subsection: 1. Irish government policy, legislation and how business influences policy

notes.b: Government policy sets out what the state intends to achieve, while legislation is binding law passed by the Oireachtas (the national parliament: the Dáil, the Seanad and the President). Businesses need to tell the two apart, because only one of them can be enforced.
points: Irish government policy means actions or statements of guidance adopted by the government and used as a basis for decision-making. In plain terms, a policy is a plan of action that sets goals and the means of reaching them, led by the Department responsible and adopted by the government.
A policy on its own creates no legal obligation, because it is a statement of intent. A firm cannot be prosecuted for ignoring a policy, but it can be penalised for breaking a law.

Legislation is law passed by the Oireachtas that binds individuals, businesses and public bodies. A Bill becomes an Act only after it passes both Houses (the Dáil and the Seanad) and is signed by the President.

Statutory instruments are secondary legislation, made by a minister under an Act to fill in the detail. For example, a minister makes detailed rules under an Act, so the Oireachtas does not have to pass a new Act for every technical change.
A policy often becomes law later: a government goal to cut emissions can be written into an Act that sets legally binding targets. The Climate Action Plan and the Act behind it are the worked case.

A new government can change policy quickly, because it needs no vote of the Oireachtas to do so. Legislation stays in force until the Oireachtas amends or repeals it, which is why it gives firms more certainty.
Do not mix up the two ideas: legislation is not a type of policy, and policy is not unimportant. It is the government's direction, and it often decides which laws are proposed.
notes.tip: If asked to distinguish policy and legislation, give at least two differences (legal force, who makes it, how easily it is changed) and an example of each. A common mistake is saying policy is not important or that legislation is a type of policy.

notes.b: Government policies do not hit every business equally, because businesses are grouped into sectors and each policy reaches some sectors more than others. Knowing the sector is the first step in explaining a policy's effect.
points: A sector of the economy is a group of producers or service providers categorised by the goods or services they output. The Central Statistics Office (CSO) publishes the list of sectors within the Irish economy.
For this topic, use plain categories: agriculture and agri-food, industry and manufacturing, construction, energy, transport, retail and wholesale, and tourism and hospitality.
One policy can reach several sectors, and one sector is affected by several policies. For example, a haulage firm in the transport sector is affected by both climate policy and carbon tax.
notes.tip: When asked to outline policies affecting different sectors, make sure each policy is tied to a different sector. A common mistake is giving two policies that hit the same sector.

notes.b: Here are six policies, each tied to the sector it reaches most, with the effect on business. Pick three for three different sectors when a question asks for them.
points: Climate Action Plan (energy, transport, buildings, industry, agriculture): the Climate Action and Low Carbon Development Act 2015, as amended in 2021, requires the plan to be updated each year. The plan is the policy and the annual update is the legal duty.

The Climate Action Plan 2025 was approved by Government in April 2025 as a roadmap to halve emissions by 2030 and reach climate neutrality by 2050. It works within carbon budgets and sectoral emissions ceilings for electricity, transport, buildings, industry and agriculture.
Carbon tax (transport and any firm using fossil fuels): a charge on fossil fuels, with increases written into law (Finance Act 2020) each year to 2030.
Because it rises on a schedule set in law, carbon tax raises fuel costs for transport firms and gives businesses a reason to invest in efficiency.

Housing (construction): 'Delivering Homes, Building Communities 2025-2030: An Action Plan on Housing Supply and Targeting Homelessness', published by Government in November 2025, aims for 300,000 new homes by the end of 2030. It succeeded Housing for All (the 2021 plan) and creates demand for builders, developers and building material suppliers.

National Development Plan (engineering and construction): the National Development Plan Review 2025, published on 22 July 2025, sets total public capital investment of EUR 275.4 billion over 2026 to 2035. It replaced the 2021-2030 plan and funds roads, public transport, water, housing and energy, which supports engineering and construction firms.

Food Vision 2030 (agri-food): launched by Government on 3 August 2021 as a ten-year strategy for primary agriculture, food and drink, fisheries, aquaculture and forestry. It aims to grow sustainable production and export value, so it affects farmers and food processors such as Kerry Group and Glanbia.

National Minimum Wage (low-paid sectors such as hospitality and retail): the National Minimum Wage Act 2000 sets the legal minimum hourly pay, and the Low Pay Commission recommends the rate each year. Any change alters labour costs in these sectors, because they employ many low-paid staff.

Policy effects are seldom one-sided, because most policies bring a cost and an opportunity together. For example, a carbon tax increase may raise a haulier's costs while giving the haulier a reason to buy electric vans.
notes.tip: To explain how a policy affects a sector, give the policy, the sector, what changes for firms (the cause) and the cost or opportunity that results. A common mistake is describing the effect on households only.

notes.h: Ethical, sustainability and digital angles of policy
notes.b: Policy does not only change business costs. It also pushes firms to act in more sustainable and fairer ways, and it increasingly works through digital tools.
points: Sustainability: climate policy and carbon tax push firms to cut emissions and to report on them, so a firm has a financial reason as well as an environmental one to change how it operates.
Sustainability and technology: a policy can require firms to adopt low-carbon technology, such as moving a delivery fleet to electric vans, which shifts what a business must invest in.
Ethics: a minimum wage is a fairness measure for workers, because it sets a floor under pay so that an employer cannot pay below the legal rate.
Digital: public consultations and the Register of Lobbying are online and searchable, so firms and citizens can take part in, and check, how policy is influenced.
notes.tip: With an unseen news headline about a new policy, identify the policy and the sector, say who gains and who loses, and add one ethical or sustainability point.

notes.b: Business shapes policy through organised groups and direct engagement, not only through voting. An interest group is an organised body that represents the shared views of a group of people or businesses to government, so it speaks for many, not for one firm.
points: Representative bodies speak for whole groups of firms. Ibec (the main employer representative body) puts employers' views to government, ISME speaks for small and medium firms, and Chambers Ireland speaks for local business communities.

Sector bodies, such as the Irish Farmers' Association and Food and Drink Industry Ireland, lobby on issues specific to their industry, so government hears about problems that general bodies might miss.
Trade unions, through the Irish Congress of Trade Unions, represent workers and take part in consultation on pay, employment law and social policy. This gives employees a voice beside employers.
Public consultations and written submissions let firms comment on draft policies before they are finalised, which means problems can be raised while the policy can still change.
Pre-Budget submissions to the Department of Finance and to Oireachtas committees can influence which tax and spending measures are included in the Budget.
Lobbying means communicating with politicians and public officials to influence a decision. It is a normal, legal part of the policy process, and it is not bribery or corruption.
Social dialogue is the continuing discussion between government, employers and trade unions on economic and social matters. It is less formal than the national partnership agreements of the past.
In one line: business informs policy with practical knowledge and influences it with organised pressure.
notes.tip: To outline business's role in national policy, cover representative bodies, consultations and submissions, lobbying, social dialogue and the lobbying register, each with how it works. Learn lobbying, interest group, policy and legislation word for word, as a sample paper has a fill-in-the-blank on interest groups and lobbying.

notes.b: Lobbying is legal, but the public used to have no way to see who was trying to influence decisions. The Regulation of Lobbying Act 2015 makes it visible by requiring registration and returns of activity.
points: The Act was signed in March 2015 and commenced on 1 September 2015. Its enforcement provisions (Part 4) commenced on 1 January 2017.

Certain lobbyists must register on the Register of Lobbying, a public record of registered lobbyists and their lobbying activity, and file returns describing the matters they lobbied on. Returns are filed three times a year, within 21 days of the end of each period.
The Register is kept by the Standards in Public Office Commission (SIPO) and can be searched by the public online at lobbying.ie. It lists lobbying activity only, not donations to parties.

The Act covers contact with designated public officials, including ministers and senior officials. Each public body must publish a list of its designated officials, and the Act places no filing duty on the officials.
Transparency lets citizens, journalists and rival interests see which groups are trying to influence a decision, which makes it harder for influence to stay hidden.
Breaches are offences, so a business that lobbies must know whether it is required to register.
notes.tip: Do not describe lobbying as corrupt, as the Act exists to make a legal activity visible. Remember that SIPO runs the Register, not the Dáil.

notes.b: Business influence can improve policy but can also distort it, so a balanced evaluation weighs both sides before reaching a judgement.
points: Advantage: business brings practical knowledge of markets, costs and jobs, which can produce policy that firms can actually implement.
Advantage: consultation gives government evidence it might not otherwise have, which can improve the quality of legislation.
Disadvantage: large firms with dedicated lobbying staff can gain more access than small firms, so policy may favour big business.
Disadvantage: consumers, workers and the environment can be under-represented when business groups dominate a debate, because they have fewer organised voices.

Interest groups compete with one another, so a proposal may face pressure from employers, unions and environmental groups at the same time. This competition can balance the influence of any single group.
notes.tip: When asked to discuss or evaluate whether business should influence policy, give advantages (evidence, workable policy) and disadvantages (unequal access, under-represented groups), then finish with a judgement. A common mistake is a one-sided list or no conclusion.

keyTerms.definition: A plan of action by the government that sets out goals and the means of achieving them.
Laws passed by the Oireachtas that bind individuals, businesses and public bodies.
Secondary legislation made by a minister under the authority of an Act to set out detailed rules.
A group of businesses that share a main activity, classified by the CSO, such as agriculture or retail.
An organised body that represents the shared views of a particular group of people or businesses to government.
Communicating with politicians and public officials in order to influence a decision.
Continuing discussion between government, employers and trade unions on economic and social matters.
A public record of registered lobbyists and their lobbying activity, maintained by the Standards in Public Office Commission.

factCards.term: Passage of a Bill into law
factCards.definition: A Bill passes through both Houses of the Oireachtas, then the President signs it and it becomes an Act.
IBEC represents employers generally, ISME represents small and medium enterprises, and Chambers Ireland represents local chambers of commerce.

factCards.term: Three routes for business to influence policy
factCards.definition: Consultation submissions, pre-Budget submissions and direct lobbying of officials and politicians.

factCards.term: Body that oversees the lobbying register
factCards.definition: The Standards in Public Office Commission.

factCards.definition: A policy states what the government intends to do; legislation is binding law that can be enforced.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between government policy and legislation, giving one Irish example of each.
questions.model: Government policy is a statement of intent that sets out what the government plans to achieve and how, but on its own it does not bind citizens or businesses. An example is Housing for All, which sets goals to increase the supply and affordability of homes up to 2030. Legislation is law passed by the Oireachtas, which is enforceable and must be obeyed. An example is the National Minimum Wage Act 2000, which sets a legal minimum hourly pay that employers must follow. The key difference is that a policy states an aim while legislation compels behaviour, although a policy goal may later be turned into an Act.

questions.prompt: Outline three Irish government policies that affect three different sectors, and explain how each affects business.
questions.model: First, the Climate Action Plan affects the energy and transport sectors. It sets emissions targets, so power generators must shift toward renewable sources, and hauliers face carbon tax costs that encourage investment in efficient or electric vehicles. Second, Food Vision 2030 affects the agri-food sector. Its aim is to grow sustainable production and export value, so farmers and processors such as Glanbia can find new export markets, although they must also meet sustainability requirements that add cost. Third, Housing for All affects the construction sector. It aims to increase the supply of homes, which creates demand for builders and developers, although planning delays and material costs can limit how quickly firms can respond. Each policy creates both opportunities and costs, and the size of the effect differs by sector.
